questions.solution_html:
• The “pull” of a goal is called its incentive value (the goal’s appeal beyond its ability to fill a
  • need). Some goals are so desirable (strawberry pie, for example) that they can motivate
  • behavior in the absence of an internal need. Incentive theories propose that external stimuli
  • regulate motivational states (Bolles, 1975; McClelland, 1975; Skinner, 1953). An incentive is
  • an external goal that has the capacity to motivate behavior Incentive theories emphasize
  • how external stimuli pull people in certain directions. According to incentive theories, the
  • source of motivation lies outside the organism, in the environment. This means that incentive
  • models don’t operate according to the principle of homeostasis, incentive theories emphasize
  • environmental factors and downplay the biological bases of human motivation.
  • Self determination theory (SDT) of Ryan and Deci (2000)there are three inborn and universal
  • needs are autonomy, or the need to be in control of one’s own behavior and goals (i.e., self
  • determination); competence, or the need to be able to master the challenging tasks of one’s
  • life; and relatedness, or the need to feel a sense of belonging, intimacy, and security in
  • relationships with others. Satisfying these needs can best be accomplished if the person has a
  • supportive environment in which to develop goals and relationships with others. Such
  • satisfaction will not only foster healthy psychological growth but also increase the
  • individual’s intrinsic motivation (actions are performed because they are internally rewarding
  • or satisfying). Evidence suggests that intrinsic motivation is increased or enhanced when a
  • person not only feels competence (through experiencing positive feedback from others and
  • succeeding at what are perceived to be challenging tasks) but also a sense of autonomy or the
  • knowledge that his or her actions are self-determined rather than controlled by others

  • on) personality as obstinate, stingy, orderly, and compulsively clean. The
  • anal-expulsive (letting-go) personality is disorderly, destructive, cruel, or messy.).

  • Complex. Fixation: immature sexual attitudes).

  • child develops in other ways, Child grow intellectually and physically).
  • Genital Stage (starts from puberty, sexual urges enters consciousness but parents are not
  • targets, individual move towards social and other adults, sexual behaviour).

questions.question: The survey method mainly relies on a). Questionnaires and interviews b). Introspection c). Observation in natural settings d). Laboratory experiments
questions.solution_html:
• of studying constancies and illusions. What are the major types of constancies and illusions?.
  • Perceptual constancy refers to the remarkable ability of the human visual system to perceive
  • objects as maintaining stable properties—such as size, shape, color, and brightness—despite
  • continuous variations in the physical sensory input reaching the retina. Perceptual illusions
  • on the other hand, occur when there is a mismatch between physical reality and our
  • subjective perception, causing us to misinterpret sensory information.
  • Perceptual constancies are categorized into three major types: Size Constancy: The
  • perception that an object retains its actual physical size regardless of changes in distance or
  • retinal image size (e.g., perceiving an approaching car as moving closer rather than growing
  • larger). Shape Constancy: The tendency to perceive a familiar object as maintaining its
  • structural form regardless of shifts in viewing angle (e.g., perceiving a door as rectangular
  • even when it swings open and casts a trapezoidal image on the retina). Brightness and Color
  • Constancy: The ability to perceive the intrinsic lightness or color of an object as constant
  • despite variations in ambient illumination (e.g., recognizing a piece of coal as black even
  • under bright sunlight).
  • Perceptual illusions fall into several primary classifications: Geometrical-Optical Illusions
  • These involve distorted spatial judgements caused by line orientation or contextual depth
  • cues. Prominent examples include the Müller-Lyer Illusion (where identical line segments
  • appear unequal due to inward- or outward-pointing arrowheads) and the Ponzo Illusion
  • (where converging linear perspective lines cause the upper horizontal line to appear longer
  • than the lower one). Ambiguous and Reversible Illusions: Displays that create figure
  • ground confusion, forcing the brain to alternate between two valid perceptual interpretations
  • such as Rubin's Vase (alternating between a vase and two facing profiles). Motion Illusions
  • Apparent motion phenomena where non-moving images generate the perception of
  • movement, such as the Phi Phenomenon or stroboscopic motion observed in animated
  • displays.
  • Students can also write other illusions and constancy according to what they have taught

questions.question: Which type of motivation arises from external rewards or punishments? a) Extrinsic motivation b) Intrinsic motivation c) Incremental motivation d) Drive motivation ( ,R)
questions.solution_html:
• autonomy.
  • Abraham Maslow proposed the hierarchy of needs, suggesting that human motivation
  • progresses from basic physiological and safety needs to love/belonging, esteem, and finally
  • self-actualization. The lower four levels are deficiency needs, activated by lack, while self
  • actualization represents a growth need driven by personal development.
  • Ryan and Deci’s Self-Determination Theory (SDT) complements Maslow’s model
  • emphasizing three innate needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—which, when
  • fulfilled in a supportive environment, enhance intrinsic motivation According to Maslow
  • autonomy is one of the meta-needs of self-actualizing individuals, representing self
  • sufficiency and independence from external pressures. Self-actualized people act according
  • to their inner values rather than social expectations.In Self-Determination Theory (Ryan &
  • Deci, 2000), autonomy is one of the three basic psychological needs—along with
  • competence and relatedness—that foster intrinsic motivation and psychological growth.
  • When individuals experience autonomy, they feel their actions are self-determined, which
  • enhances motivation, creativity, and overall well-being.

questions.question: Differentiate Maslow’s self-actualization and Self-determination theory's concept of autonomy.

  • Abraham Maslow proposed the hierarchy of needs, suggesting that human motivation
  • progresses from basic physiological and safety needs to love/belonging, esteem, and finally
  • self-actualization. The lower four levels are deficiency needs, activated by lack, while self
  • actualization represents a growth need driven by personal development.
  • Ryan and Deci’s Self-Determination Theory (SDT) complements Maslow’s model
  • emphasizing three innate needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—which, when
  • fulfilled in a supportive environment, enhance intrinsic motivation According to Maslow

  • sufficiency and independence from external pressures. Self-actualized people act according
  • to their inner values rather than social expectations.In Self-Determination Theory (Ryan &
  • Deci, 2000), autonomy is one of the three basic psychological needs—along with
  • competence and relatedness—that foster intrinsic motivation and psychological growth.
  • When individuals experience autonomy, they feel their actions are self-determined, which
  • enhances motivation, creativity, and overall well-being.

questions.question: State the Yerkes–Dodson law.
questions.solution_html:
• The Yerkes–Dodson Law describes an empirical, inverted U-shaped relationship between
  • physiological or mental arousal and performance efficiency. Developed by psychologists
  • Robert Yerkes and John Dillingham Dodson, the law states that performance increases with
  • physiological or cognitive arousal, but only up to an optimal threshold. When arousal levels
  • fall below this optimal point, a person experiences boredom, apathy, or low motivation
  • leading to suboptimal performance. Conversely, when arousal exceeds the optimal level
  • extreme anxiety, stress, or sensory overload impairs cognitive capacity and motor execution
  • causing performance to deteriorate rapidly.
  • “Level of arousal beyond which performance begin to decline is a function of task difficulty”

  • perceiving the surrounding world .Feature analysis assumes that form perception involves

  • processing, a progression from the whole to the elements.

questions.question: Explain in detail the trait theories of personality.

• Gordon Allport pioneered this approach by categorizing traits into cardinal (rare, dominant
  • drives), central (core building blocks of character), and secondary (situational preferences)
  • levels. Moving toward quantitative measurement, Raymond Cattell used factor analysis to
  • distinguish observable surface traits from 16 fundamental, underlying source traits
  • measured by the 16PF. Hans Eysenck further simplified trait theory into a biologically rooted
  • PEN model, focusing on Psychoticism, Extraversion–Introversion, and Neuroticism
  • Emotional Stability. Today, personality research is dominated by Costa and McCrae’s Five

questions.question: Compare incentive theory and Self determination theory of motivation.
questions.solution_html:
• The “pull” of a goal is called its incentive value (the goal’s appeal beyond its ability to fill a
  • need). Some goals are so desirable (strawberry pie, for example) that they can motivate
  • behavior in the absence of an internal need. Incentive theories propose that external stimuli
  • regulate motivational states (Bolles, 1975; McClelland, 1975; Skinner, 1953). An incentive is
  • an external goal that has the capacity to motivate behavior Incentive theories emphasize
  • how external stimuli pull people in certain directions. According to incentive theories, the
  • source of motivation lies outside the organism, in the environment. This means that incentive
  • models don’t operate according to the principle of homeostasis, incentive theories emphasize
  • environmental factors and downplay the biological bases of human motivation.
  • Self determination theory (SDT) of Ryan and Deci (2000)there are three inborn and universal
  • needs are autonomy, or the need to be in control of one’s own behavior and goals (i.e., self
  • determination); competence, or the need to be able to master the challenging tasks of one’s
  • life; and relatedness, or the need to feel a sense of belonging, intimacy, and security in
  • relationships with others. Satisfying these needs can best be accomplished if the person has a
  • supportive environment in which to develop goals and relationships with others. Such
  • satisfaction will not only foster healthy psychological growth but also increase the
  • individual’s intrinsic motivation (actions are performed because they are internally rewarding
  • or satisfying). Evidence suggests that intrinsic motivation is increased or enhanced when a
  • person not only feels competence (through experiencing positive feedback from others and
  • succeeding at what are perceived to be challenging tasks) but also a sense of autonomy or the
  • knowledge that his or her actions are self-determined rather than controlled by others

questions.question: Define and explain perceptual constancy and perceptual illusions. Explain the importance of studying constancies and illisions.What are the major types of constancies and illusions?
questions.solution_html:
• Perceptual constancy refers to the remarkable ability of the human visual system to perceive
  • objects as maintaining stable properties—such as size, shape, color, and brightness—despite
  • continuous variations in the physical sensory input reaching the retina. Perceptual illusions
  • on the other hand, occur when there is a mismatch between physical reality and our
  • subjective perception, causing us to misinterpret sensory information.
  • Perceptual constancies are categorized into three major types: Size Constancy: The
  • perception that an object retains its actual physical size regardless of changes in distance or
  • retinal image size (e.g., perceiving an approaching car as moving closer rather than growing
  • larger). Shape Constancy: The tendency to perceive a familiar object as maintaining its
  • structural form regardless of shifts in viewing angle (e.g., perceiving a door as rectangular
  • even when it swings open and casts a trapezoidal image on the retina). Brightness and Color
  • Constancy: The ability to perceive the intrinsic lightness or color of an object as constant
  • despite variations in ambient illumination (e.g., recognizing a piece of coal as black even
  • under bright sunlight).
  • Perceptual illusions fall into several primary classifications: Geometrical-Optical Illusions
  • These involve distorted spatial judgements caused by line orientation or contextual depth
  • cues. Prominent examples include the Müller-Lyer Illusion (where identical line segments
  • appear unequal due to inward- or outward-pointing arrowheads) and the Ponzo Illusion
  • (where converging linear perspective lines cause the upper horizontal line to appear longer
  • than the lower one). Ambiguous and Reversible Illusions: Displays that create figure
  • ground confusion, forcing the brain to alternate between two valid perceptual interpretations
  • such as Rubin's Vase (alternating between a vase and two facing profiles). Motion Illusions
  • Apparent motion phenomena where non-moving images generate the perception of
  • movement, such as the Phi Phenomenon or stroboscopic motion observed in animated
  • displays.
  • Students can also write other illusions and constancy according to what they have taught
